hero.headline: Shopify vs Ecwid
hero.subheadline: A side-by-side comparison for buyers, operators, and affiliate-content readers.

summary.best_for_a: Shopify is best for merchants who need a scalable, full-featured store with a large app ecosystem and built-in payments.
summary.best_for_b: Ecwid is best for small businesses that want an affordable, easy-to-embed store to add commerce to existing websites and social channels.
summary.quick_take: Shopify delivers a powerful, end-to-end e-commerce platform built for growth: advanced storefront controls, a huge app marketplace, native payment processing, and robust POS options. Ecwid focuses on simplicity and flexibility for smaller sellers—installable on any site, light on setup, and budget-friendly—but it lacks the depth of customization and scalability that larger merchants typically need.

rows.tool_a: Tiered plans with more features at higher price points; apps and transaction fees can increase total cost.
rows.tool_b: Lower starting cost and free plan available; paid tiers remain affordable for small catalogs with fewer added fees.

rows.tool_a: Intuitive admin for everyday tasks but many advanced settings and app integrations require a learning curve.
rows.tool_b: Very straightforward setup and embedding; minimal configuration required to start selling.

rows.tool_a: Extensive theme library, customization options, and advanced commerce features for complex stores.
rows.tool_b: Basic but effective storefront features; customization is more limited and relies on simpler templates.

rows.tool_a: Designed to scale from small shops to enterprise-level operations with performance and multi-store options.
rows.tool_b: Ideal for small to mid-size merchants; not intended for large enterprise scaling.

rows.tool_a: Huge app marketplace covering marketing, fulfillment, accounting, and more.
rows.tool_b: Solid integrations for common platforms and social channels but far fewer third-party apps.

rows.tool_a: Native payment gateway with competitive rates; third-party gateways supported but may incur extra fees.
rows.tool_b: Supports many payment processors with transparent pricing; fewer native payment features.

rows.tool_a: Robust POS system and omnichannel tools for in-person, online, and social selling.
rows.tool_b: Can sell across channels and marketplaces, but its POS and omnichannel capabilities are more basic.

rows.tool_a: Strong SEO controls and marketing apps for growth-focused merchants.
rows.tool_b: Covers essential SEO and marketing needs; fewer advanced optimization tools.

rows.tool_a: 24/7 global support, large community, and extensive documentation and developer resources.
rows.tool_b: Responsive support and helpful guides; smaller community and fewer developer resources.

rows.tool_a: You plan to scale, need advanced features, or want a unified commerce stack.
rows.tool_b: You want to add a store to an existing site quickly and affordably without managing a full platform.

paragraphs: Comparing Shopify and Ecwid helps merchants decide between a dedicated, scalable e-commerce platform and a lightweight store that embeds into existing sites. Both let you sell products online, but they take different approaches to features, pricing, and growth.
When picking between them, evaluate monthly cost, available integrations, customization and design control, built-in payment and POS options, and how easy it is to maintain as your business grows.

data.headline: Shopify for growth, Ecwid for simplicity and embedding
data.summary: Choose Shopify if you plan to scale, need a wide app ecosystem, or want a native payments and POS solution. Choose Ecwid if you need a low-cost, easy-to-add storefront for an existing site, social channels, or multiple sales locations without the complexity of a full platform.

pros: Comprehensive feature set with advanced store customization and themes
Large app marketplace and built-in payment/POS options for omnichannel sales
cons: Higher monthly and app-related costs can add up for small businesses
Steeper learning curve for deep customization and advanced workflows

pros: Low-cost, fast setup and easy embedding on existing websites and social pages
Simple inventory and multichannel selling without a full platform overhaul
cons: Fewer advanced features, apps, and limited storefront customization compared to major platforms
Scalability and enterprise features are limited for high-growth merchants

tool_a: Best-in-class scalability, app ecosystem, and omnichannel commerce
tool_b: Fast, affordable embeddable store for existing sites and social selling

items.question: Which platform is cheaper to start with, Shopify or Ecwid?
items.answer: Ecwid is generally cheaper to start with thanks to a free tier and lower-paid plans; Shopify offers more built-in features but can be more expensive once you add apps and payment fees.

items.question: Can I use Ecwid with an existing website?
items.answer: Yes — Ecwid is designed to embed easily into existing websites, WordPress, Wix, and social channels so you can add commerce without rebuilding your site.

items.question: Is Shopify better for in-person sales and POS?
items.answer: Shopify has a robust POS system with hardware and advanced omnichannel features, making it a stronger choice for merchants who sell in-person as well as online.

items.question: Can I migrate from Ecwid to Shopify later?
items.answer: Yes — product and customer data can be migrated from Ecwid to Shopify, though the process may require data cleanup and setup of themes and apps on the new platform.

items.question: Which platform offers more extensions and third-party apps?
items.answer: Shopify has a much larger app marketplace with extensive third-party add-ons for marketing, fulfillment, analytics, and more; Ecwid has fewer apps focused on core small-business needs.
